title: Linear-T resistivity: strange-metal evidence and model limits
summary: Read linear-temperature transport with its fit window, field and carrier assumptions. Distinguish total resistivity, parallel conduction channels and inferred scattering rates.

review.scope: Pinned A8 chapter; selected published Cao passages, Legros/Romero earlier manuscripts and Martin abstract; independent fit-window, Drude-degeneracy, parallel-channel and frequency-convention checks.
limitations: Selected checks are not full scientific acceptance, experimental replication or complete uncertainty propagation.
Legros and Romero earlier manuscript passages are version-specific; exhaustive comparison with final published articles remains open.
Cooper and Bruin are bibliographic pointers only; no cross-family numerical alpha table reproduced.
Synthetic model checks do not identify a material mechanism. No equilibrium Tc is inferred from normal-state transport.

claims.statement: Linear-temperature resistivity describes a measured dependence over a specified range. The fit $\rho(T)=\rho_0+AT$ needs a sample, current direction, field, temperature interval and residuals. A straight-looking trace is not by itself evidence for a quantum critical point, a universal lifetime or a pairing interaction. This entry treats transport phenomenology; the linked Planckian entry discusses lifetime interpretations.
claims.conditions: Editorial reporting and inference criteria; no universal lifetime, pairing mechanism or transition temperature follows from a fitted slope.
claims.verificationScope: Pinned A8 chapter edited with explicit source/model limitations.

claims.statement: Separate a finite-field normal state, the region affected by superconducting fluctuations, and a higher-temperature regime that may have different scattering. Martin and colleagues' Bi-based crystal abstract reports strongly anisotropic transport; an in-plane trend is not an isotropic resistivity law.
claims.conditions: Sample-, probe-, field-, fit-window- and version-specific observations; no material-independent coefficient or new equilibrium Tc record.

claims.statement: For a single isotropic Drude channel with temperature-independent carrier density $n$ and mass $m^*$, an inelastic pole relaxation rate $\gamma=\alpha k_BT/\hbar$ gives $A=\alpha m^*k_B/(ne^2\hbar)$. Thus a slope fixes $\alpha$ only after the carrier parameters and response model are specified. If those parameters change with temperature, differentiating resistivity produces additional terms. This conditional connection underlies the selected Legros analysis.

claims.statement: The total slope is generally temperature dependent even though the first channel's resistance is exactly linear. Nine numerical derivative checks verify this model. It is not a multiband fit; in magnetic field, conductivity tensors must be added before inversion. Adding scattering mechanisms within one channel is a different assumption from adding parallel conductivities.

claims.statement: Legros and colleagues' earlier manuscript measures a Bi2212 film with nominal hole doping 0.23 in pulsed fields. Its 55 T trace and magnetoresistance-corrected, extrapolated zero-field curve are distinct datasets. The analysis estimates carrier parameters and geometric uncertainty; the checked passages do not turn its interpretation into a model-independent universal bound.

claims.statement: Cao and colleagues measure four-probe transport in gated twisted bilayer graphene. Their linear regime depends on filling and a crossover temperature. The operational scattering coefficient uses density and mass from low-temperature quantum oscillations; those assumptions matter when interpreting higher-temperature transport. The selected passages do not establish one shared microscopic mechanism across material families.

claims.statement: Romero and colleagues' earlier manuscript studies two 100 nm FeTe1-xSex films, x = 0.45 and 0.35, over 0.2–3 THz. Its narrow-channel fits use 20–40 K and report coefficients 3.02 and 2.42 in $\Gamma=\Gamma_0+\alpha k_BT/h$. These are channel-specific fit results, not coefficients of the total DC resistivity.

claims.statement:
Frequency conventions can create a factor-of-$2\pi$ error. For a Drude denominator $\Gamma-i
u$ with ordinary frequency $
u$, the corresponding pole rate is $\gamma=1/	au=2\pi\Gamma$ in a denominator $\gamma-i\omega$, where $\omega=2\pi
u$. Consequently $\Gamma=\alpha k_BT/h$ converts to $\gamma=\alpha k_BT/\hbar$. State the denominator and linewidth convention before comparing coefficients. This is a convention check, not a new measurement of a lifetime.

claims.statement: A shared temperature exponent does not identify a unique microscopic interaction. Drude transport, optical fits and single-particle lifetimes measure or infer different quantities. Extrapolating carrier parameters, suppressing superconductivity by field, or neglecting a parallel channel can affect an inferred coefficient. Report these choices alongside any claimed universality rather than treating the fit exponent as a proof.

claims.statement: Use linear-T transport to organize experiments, not to rank superconductors or predict a transition temperature by itself. A stronger comparison holds sample state, probe definition and fitting procedure fixed, then asks whether independent optical, thermodynamic or quantum-oscillation information supports the same parameter interpretation. Retain counterexamples and failed fits; correlation with superconductivity does not identify its cause.
